legend: Alice got an array of length n%%ZSMJ0%% as a birthday present once again! This is the third year in a row!
And what is more disappointing, it is overwhelmengly boring, filled entirely with zeros. Bob decided to apply some changes to the array to cheer up Alice.

Bob has chosen m%%ZSMJ1%% changes of the following form. For some integer numbers x%%ZSMJ2%% and d%%ZSMJ3%%, he chooses an arbitrary position i%%ZSMJ4%% (1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ5%%) and for every j∈[1,n]%%ZSMJ6%% adds x+d⋅dist(i,j)%%ZSMJ7%% to the value of the j%%ZSMJ8%%-th cell. dist(i,j)%%ZSMJ9%% is the distance between positions i%%ZSMJ10%% and j%%ZSMJ11%% (i.e. dist(i,j)=|i−j|%%ZSMJ12%%, where |x|%%ZSMJ13%% is an absolute value of x%%ZSMJ14%%).

For example, if Alice currently has an array [2,1,2,2]%%ZSMJ15%% and Bob chooses position 3%%ZSMJ16%% for x=−1%%ZSMJ17%% and d=2%%ZSMJ18%% then the array will become [2−1+2⋅2, 1−1+2⋅1, 2−1+2⋅0, 2−1+2⋅1]%%ZSMJ19%% = [5,2,1,3]%%ZSMJ20%%. Note that Bob can't choose position i%%ZSMJ21%% outside of the array (that is, smaller than 1%%ZSMJ22%% or greater than n%%ZSMJ23%%).
Alice will be the happiest when the elements of the array are as big as possible. Bob claimed that the arithmetic mean value of the elements will work fine as a metric.
What is the maximum arithmetic mean value Bob can achieve?
input: The first line contains two integers n%%ZSMJ24%% and m%%ZSMJ25%% (1≤n,m≤105%%ZSMJ26%%) — the number of elements of the array and the number of changes.
Each of the next m%%ZSMJ27%% lines contains two integers xi%%ZSMJ28%% and di%%ZSMJ29%% (−103≤xi,di≤103%%ZSMJ30%%) — the parameters for the i%%ZSMJ31%%-th change.
output: Print the maximal average arithmetic mean of the elements Bob can achieve.
Your answer is considered correct if its absolute or relative error doesn't exceed 10−6%%ZSMJ32%%.
